# Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta (MN 46 (PTS MN i 309))

**ID:** MN 46 (PTS MN i 309)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Great Discourse on Taking Up Practices
**PTS:** MN i 309
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn46
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta* ("The Greater Discourse on Ways of Undertaking Things") is the forty-sixth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthi [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Addressed to the monks, it opens with their affirmation that their teachings have the Blessed One as their source, guide, and resort (*bhagavammūlakā no bhante dhammā bhagavamnettikā bhagavampaṭisaraṇā*) [Marciniak 2019]. Like its companion discourse, the *Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta* (MN 45), the sutta expounds four ways of taking up practices or undertaking things, distinguishing them based on whether they are painful or pleasant in the present and whether they ripen in pain or pleasure in the future [Humphreys 1956; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse examines how conduct and views—such as abstaining from or engaging in killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and wrong view—shape one's experiential results and determine future rebirths [Anderson 1999; Rogell 2003].

In the Theravāda commentarial tradition recorded in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the sutta is noted as having been recited at night by a young monk at Paṅgura-vihāra in southern Ceylon (Hatthibhogajanapada), an enchanting recitation that pleased a listening deity (*devatā*) into voicing praise [Adikaram 1946; Rahula 1956].

Curated full parallels to the sutta include two Chinese translations: Madhyama Āgama discourse MĀ 175 and the individual translation T 83 (*Yingfa jing*, 應法經) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus aligns the sutta closely with T 83 and the *Madhyama Āgama* (ZH_T01_0026), corroborating these parallels, and indicates cross-language text reuse with Sanskrit and Tibetan canonical materials [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records extensive shared passages with MN 45, as well as significant textual overlaps with several sections of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 10, AN 5, AN 3, AN 4) and *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 12, SN 35) [DharmaNexus].
